To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the field-scale acetation of groundwater reduced the soluble U concentration in the groundwater, and the acetate was utilized by a variety of microbes in the groundwater and on the solid phases.
Geobacter-like organisms were the primary (13)C-acetate-utilizing bacteria in the groundwater before and after field-scale acetate injection.
the acetate-utilizing bacterial populations in the Rifle IFRC site are highly dynamic and can shift from one phase (e.g. groundwater, sand, fines) to another in a relatively short period of time.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the biodegradation and biotransformation of organic compounds and metals in the subsurface environment, and how the microbial community structure influences the biogeochemistry.
the use of acetate as an energy source for the reduction of uranium(VI) to U(IV) by bacteria in the subsurface.
understanding the role that microbial activity plays in the mobilization and immobilization of uranium at a field site.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the acetate-utilizing microbial community at the Rifle site was dominated by the Geobacteraceae, with a minor contribution from the Dechloromonas/Acinetobacter group.

acetate utilization by the active bacteria was primarily particle-associated, and the Geobacter sp. were more active after acetate field additions, while the other active bacterial groups were less active.
the acetate utilization by the active bacteria in the Rifle, CO IFRC site was strongly phase-dependent and was affected by the addition of acetate.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the addition of acetate stimulated the activity of a Geobacter sp. on sand and fines particles, while the Acinetobacter and D. sp. were stimulated in groundwater.

the acetate-utilizing microbial communities at Rifle, CO were very different from the ones in the laboratory, and the field-scale addition of the carbon source did not lead to a simple, predictable response by the microbes.
acetate addition in the field resulted in an increase of the Geobacter sp. on sand and fines and a decrease of the alpha Proteobacter and Dechloromonas-like bacteria.
The main takeaway from our work is that
(13)C-AP was able to detect the activity of bacteria on solid phases, and that the activity of the Geobacter sp. was not limited to the groundwater, but was also found in the solid phases.
the field-scale acetation addition resulted in a change in the dominant acetate utilizing microbes.
(13)C stable isotope probing of DNA is useful for identifying microbes in a field-scale setting and for understanding the role of microbes in the bioremediation of uranium-contaminated groundwater.
